name: Reminders That Work, and Reminders That Do Not
title: Reminders That Work, and Reminders That Do Not
answer: Reminders about college and financial aid steps work best when they come from someone the student knows, such as their own counselor, rather than from a large outside campaign. Several large trials found that messages sent at scale by unfamiliar organizations had little or no effect, while counselor-sent texts raised college steps and enrollment for some students. AI can help counselors personalize and send reminders at a scale they could not manage by hand, but the relationship and the counselor's judgment remain central.

sections.body: This idea is about who sends a reminder and what it says, not just how many students it reaches. Large campaigns that send the same message from an outside organization often fail to move students toward college or financial aid, even when they reach hundreds of thousands of people. Students respond to people they know, so a message from their own counselor carries weight that a national mailing does not. The problem it solves is wasted effort: schools and programs spend money and time on broad reminders that do not change behavior. The fix is to send messages through an existing relationship and to name the student's actual next step.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, a counselor can draft reminders about upcoming deadlines and use the school's texting platform to send them to the right students. Each message should name the student's real next step, such as submitting a transcript or finishing a financial aid form, and should include the counselor's name and a way to reply so it feels personal. Deadline tracking tools such as Scoir and BigFuture let students keep track of applications and deadlines, and let the counselor see who is behind and reach out. The tool holds the list, while the counselor holds the relationship. The text does not give separate grade band guidance, so the practice applies wherever students are working on college and financial aid steps.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with evidence from several large trials. In Texas, text messages from students' own counselors raised college steps and enrollment for some groups of students (Avery et al., 2021). A national campaign sending similar messages from an outside organization had mostly no effect. Two trials of national and state financial aid campaigns reached about 800,000 students and found no effect on aid or enrollment (Bird et al., 2021). A national trial with 785,000 students tested brochures, emails, texts, and application fee waivers to encourage enrollment at selective colleges, and it too found no change (Gurantz et al., 2020).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits. Scale alone does not produce results, so sending more messages from an unfamiliar source is not a fix. Messages must reach students through a relationship and address their specific situation, which means a generic reminder is likely to be ignored. The tool keeps the list, but the counselor keeps the relationship, so the human connection and the counselor's judgment about who needs help stay with a person. The text does not describe legal duties or privacy rules, and this page describes practice rather than legal advice.
